Learning Objectives
Identify the mechanism of injury of patellar fractures.
Diagnose a patellar sleeve fracture in young children.
Differentiate a patellar fracture from a bipartite patella.
Discuss the indications for surgical management of patellar fractures and the concept of the
tension band technique.
Recognize potential complications of patellar fractures, especially implant prominence and
irritation.
Determine the workup for tibial spine fractures and indications for surgical management.

limitations.

Patellar Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Overview
Fractures of the patella are rare in children; the focus of this lesson is mostly on patellar sleeve
fractures.
Epidemiology

Epidemiology
Patellar fractures are rare in children, with an incidence of around 0.44%.1 Patellar
sleeve fractures occur in patients aged 8 to 12 years and make up most pediatric patellar
fractures.2,3
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
In young children, the patella may not be fully ossified; therefore, injury may result in a
chondral (or osteochondral) avulsion, termed a patellar sleeve fracture, rather than a fracture
of the osseous body of the patella.

Osteology

Osteology
The patella is a sesamoid that begins to ossify via endochondral ossification between
ages 3 and 6 years. Once fully mature, the proximal 75% of the posterior surface is
covered by articular cartilage. This is the thickest articular cartilage in the body. The
major medial and lateral facets are separated by a vertical ridge, and as many as seven
distinct facets may be identified in most individuals; however, young children with an
incompletely ossified patella may be vulnerable to injury.
Vascular Anatomy
The vascular supply to the patella comes from an anastomotic ring from the geniculate
arteries. The inferior pole contains the most important supply.
Tendons
The patella serves as the sesamoid attachment point of the quadriceps tendon superiorly and
the patellar tendon distally.
Joints and Ligaments
The patella articulates with the trochlea of the distal femur to form the patellofemoral joint.
The retinaculum and the medial patellofemoral ligament are among the structures that
stabilize the patella within the trochlea.
Musculature
The quadriceps musculature flexes the knee via its attachment on the patella.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Patellar sleeve fractures typically result from eccentric loading during resisted knee flexion
with quadriceps contraction, causing the patella to fail in tension.

Patellar body fractures may occur secondary to direct impact, and marginal avulsion fractures
may occur during patellar dislocation events.
Injury Classification
Categorized based on location, fracture configuration, and amount of displacement
Patellar sleeve fractures are a type of patellar fracture that is unique to children and occur if a
chondral sleeve of the patella separates from the main portion of the patella and ossific
nucleus (Figure 1).
Figure 1 Lateral view illustration of a knee shows a patellar sleeve fracture. The only sign
observed on plain radiographs may be patella alta. (Adapted with permission from Tolo VT:
Fractures and dislocations around the knee, in Green NE, Swiontkowski MF, eds: Skeletal Trauma
in Children. Philadelphia, PA, WB Saunders, 1994, vol 3, pp 369-395.)
Mechanics of Fractures
Fracture displacement is the result of the pull of the quadriceps and patellar tendons.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patellar fractures need to be differentiated from a bipartite patella.
A bipartite patella is a normal variant (in ≤5% of knees) and differs from a patellar fracture in
two ways:

A bipartite patella has rounded, well-defined borders.
A bipartite patella typically is located superolaterally (type III bipartite). An inferior pole
bipartite (type I) is least common and presents with chronic rather than acute symptoms and
little to no swelling.
Patient History
A patient history of trauma, knee effusion, inability to actively extend the knee, high riding
patella, and occasionally a palpable gap increase suspicion for a patellar fracture.
Patients typically have a notable effusion and tenderness to palpation about the patella.
Often, a palpable gap is within the patella, and difficulty with straight leg raise or with active
knee extension, is observed.
Children with a patellar sleeve fracture frequently have patella alta.

Patient History
In general, patients with an acute patella body or a sleeve fracture have a large effusion.
A palpable bony defect may be noted in patients with a fracture of the patellar body, and
patients likely will have substantial pain with range of motion. Young children with a
patellar sleeve fracture also may have patella alta because of the pull of the quadriceps
tendon. Clinically, this can be compared with the contralateral knee. Evaluation of knee
extensor mechanism integrity is a crucial aspect of the physical examination. This is
assessed by asking the patient to actively extend the knee and/or perform a straight leg
raise. This also should be tested with gravity eliminated. To do this, the patient is placed
in the lateral decubitus position and asked to actively extend the knee. Pain or effusion
may limit the physical examination, even with gravity eliminated. In such patients,
aspiration of hemarthrosis and/or injection of local anesthetic may be considered.
Imaging Studies
Radiography
Radiographs often are sufficient to identify and characterize patellar fractures. SEND FEEDBACK


Radiography
For patellar sleeve fractures, the only finding observed on plain radiographs may be
patella alta for distal fractures or patella baja for proximal pole fractures, which are less
common. Therefore, these fractures may bemissed during initial presentation by
surgeons unfamiliar with the injury pattern (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Preoperative lateral radiograph (A), intraoperative lateral fluoroscopic image
(B), and postoperative lateral radiograph (C) of a knee show a patellar sleeve fracture.
(Courtesy of Neeraj M. Patel, MD, Chicago, IL.)
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI rarely is indicated but can provide detail of the chondro-osseous anatomy in patients in
whom a patellar sleeve fracture is suspected, especially if the patient is unable to cooperate
with a complete knee examination because of pain.
Ultrasonography
Ultrasonography may aid in diagnosis if physical examination and radiographs are unclear in
patients in whom a patellar sleeve fracture is suspected.
Ultrasonography may be a quicker and less costly alternative to MRI.
Differential Diagnosis
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:33 PM
AAOS | Patellar Fractures, Tibial Spine (Eminence) Fractures, Tibial and Fibular Fractures
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000581
6/39

The differential diagnosis includes quadriceps and patellar tendon ruptures; however, these
are exceedingly rare in the pediatric population. Patellofemoral dislocation also may be
considered in the differential diagnosis.
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management is indicated for nondisplaced and minimally displaced fractures
(articular displacement <2 mm) in children without extensor lag.4 In general, vertical fracture
patterns also are amenable to nonsurgical management.
Contraindications
A disrupted extensor mechanism and/or more than 2 mm of articular displacement are
contraindications to nonsurgical management. Patellar sleeve fractures typically require
surgical management.
Techniques/Procedures
The leg is immobilized in extension with the use of a long leg cast, cylinder cast, or brace.
Weight bearing as tolerated typically is allowed.
Surgical Management
Indications
Patellar fractures displaced more than 2 mm at the articular surface should be managed
surgically. The indication for surgical management is confirmed by an extensor lag or the
inability to actively extend the knee.
Patellar sleeve fractures require surgical management, especially if the extensor mechanism is
dysfunctional.
Contraindications
Nondisplaced or minimally displaced fractures with an intact extensor mechanism do not
require surgical management. Typically, vertical fracture patterns also are amenable to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:33 PM

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000581
7/39

nonsurgical management.
Techniques/Procedures
For osseous fractures, fixation via tension banding; a cerclage wire may be necessary for
extensively comminuted fractures.
Additional details on the management of patellar body fractures are discussed in the lesson on
adult patella fractures.
For patellar sleeve fractures, the avulsed sleeve is repaired to its origin via suture repair.

Techniques/Procedures
Transosseous drill holes or suture anchors may be used to manage patellar sleeve
fractures (Figure 3). When creating transosseous drill holes, care should be taken to
avoid penetration of the articular cartilage or the anterior patellar cortex.
Nonabsorbable suture is passed through the patellar tendon and the avulsed chondral
sleeve. The tails of these sutures are then passed through the transosseous tunnels and
tied to approximate the sleeve to the inferior patella. Alternatively, suture anchors can
be used in lieu of transosseous tunnels. The torn retinaculum also is repaired to further
restore the integrity of the extensor mechanism.

repaired with the use of a combination of transosseous sutures and a suture anchor.
(Courtesy of Neeraj M. Patel, MD, MPH, MBS, Chicago, IL.)
Complications
After surgical fixation of transosseous (body) fractures, symptomatic implants are the most
common complication and may require revision surgery for removal.
Other postoperative complications may include anterior knee pain, osteonecrosis, infection,
stiffness, extensor weakness/lag, or nonunion.
Outcomes
Little data are available on the long-term outcomes of children with a patellar fracture;
however, most patients are thought to do well with appropriate treatment.1,3

Pearls and Pitfalls
Poor extensor strength or extensor lag after subacute injury in skeletally immature patients
with grossly normal radiographs should prompt additional investigation for possible patellar
sleeve fracture.
Tibial Spine (Eminence) Fractures
Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Tibial spine fractures are relatively rare.

Epidemiology
Fractures of the tibial spine occur in approximately 3 per 100,000 children annually. They
account for 2% to 5% of pediatric knee injuries with effusion. These fractures are more
common in skeletally immature patients aged 8 to 14 years. Because of the rarity of this
injury and nonspecific physical examination findings, diagnosis may be delayed or
missed.
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The tibial spine is the most prominent aspect within the tibial epiphyseal footprint that serves
as the attachment point for the anterior cruciate ligament (ACL).

Osteology
In children and young adolescents, the tibial spine may not be fully ossified. Therefore,
the partially ossified tibial spine may fracture before rupture of the ACL if patients
SEND FEEDBACK

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000581
10/39

sustain a knee injury. In addition, variable loading rate and density of the cancellous
epiphyseal bone may play a role.
Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
The mechanism of injury typically is external tibial rotation with forced knee flexion.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Because the tibial spine is the attachment point of the ACL, the mechanism of tibial spine
fractures is similar to that of ACL rupture. This often involves a hyperextension injury or
internal rotation of the tibia with knee valgus. Historically, fractures of the tibial spine
were most commonly observed in patients with bicycle injuries; however, given the
drastic increase in youth sports participation, this fracture commonly is sustained during
soccer, rugby, skiing, and other sports with noncontact injuries.
Associated Injuries
A relatively high number of children with a tibial spine fracture also may have meniscal tears,
cartilage injuries, or bone bruising. Partial injury to the ACL also may be observed.

Associated Injuries
The exact rate of concomitant injuries in patients with a tibial spine fracture varies in the
literature. Meniscal tears may be observed in 29% to 40%, bone bruising may be
observed in 68% to 90%, and non-ACL ligamentous injury may be observed in 32% of
patients with a tibial spine fracture.5,6 This likely is because the mechanism of injury is
similar to that of ACL rupture, with which such concomitant injuries also are common.
Although full-thickness ACL rupture is rare in patients with a tibial spine fracture, partial
tears or subtle elongation of the ACL occasionally may be observed.

Injury Classification
The Meyers and McKeever classification of tibial spine fractures is used (Figure 4).
Type I is minimally displaced, type II is hinged with displacement of the anterior portion, and
type III is completely displaced.


Injury Classification
The Meyers and McKeever classification system is commonly used in categorizing tibial
spine fractures; however, it recently has been questioned regarding its reliability. Debate
exists regarding the reproducibility of the classification system and its ability to guide
management or predict prognosis.7
Mechanics of Fractures
Because the ACL attaches to the tibial spine, superior displacement or angulation typically is
present because of the pull of the ACL. A displaced fracture also may result in a mechanical
block to knee extension.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Children with fractures of the tibial spine present with a mechanism of injury consistent with
an ACL tear and an acutely unstable knee.
Patient History
Patients may report a mechanism of injury similar to that of an ACL tear.

Similar to ACL injuries, the mechanism of injury may include contact or noncontact
injuries. Pain and effusion are the most common symptoms. Some patients also may
report instability, difficulty with weight bearing or motion, or mechanical symptoms (ie,
locking or catching).

Physical Examination
The physical examination is comparable to that after an ACL tear; however, some maneuvers
may be difficult to perform because of the presence of an intra-articular fracture.

Physical Examination
Joint line tenderness, if present, may be related to meniscal injury. Anterior drawer,
Lachman, and pivot-shift tests often are difficult to perform in the acutely injured knee.
Attention should be paid to the patient’s arc of motion because inability to fully extend
the knee may be because of a displaced fracture, a large hemarthrosis, or other intra-
articular injury.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs are key in identifying the injury. MRI aids identifying associated injuries, such
as injuries to the meniscus or the fibers of the ACL.
Radiography
Plain radiographs of the knee are the first imaging study required for a suspected tibial spine
fracture (Figure 5).

III tibial spine fracture. (Courtesy of Neeraj M. Patel, MD, MPH, MBS, Chicago, IL.)

Radiography
Scrutiny of knee radiographs is required for any child with an effusion after an acute
injury. Because tibial spine fractures are relatively uncommon, they may be easily missed
if imaging studies are not evaluated closely. A lateral radiograph of the knee is especially
important in characterizing the fracture.
Computed Tomography
CT typically does not add additional information in children with a tibial spine fracture because
it cannot identify concomitant soft-tissue injury.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI helps identify concomitant injuries and may aid in guiding management (Figure 6).
Figure 6 Sagittal T2-weighted MRIs of the knee of a 13-year-old girl show a tear in the posterior
horn of the lateral meniscus (A) associated with an avulsion fracture of the tibial spine (B).


Magnetic Resonance Imaging
Concomitant injuries are relatively common. These typically consist of meniscal or
cartilage pathology. Bone bruising or ligamentous injury also may be present. MRI may
aid in the diagnosis of these injuries, the presence of which may affect treatment
decisions.
Differential Diagnosis
The differential diagnosis for a tibial spine fracture includes ACL tear, meniscal tear, chondral
injury, or other intra-articular injury.
A tibial spine fracture may be mistaken for an intra-articular loose osteochondral fracture, or
the inverse can occur (ie, patellar osteochondral fracture).
Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management may be indicated for type I and some type II fractures. For type II
fractures, reduction must be within a few millimeters of anatomic to accept closed
management.8

Indications
Debate exists regarding indications for surgical or nonsurgical management of type II
fractures. Some surgeons will obtain a radiograph with the knee in extension to
determine if a type II fracture will subsequently improve in position. Alternatively, if MRI

in patients with a type II fracture, some surgeons may consider surgical management.
Contraindications
Type III or irreducible type II fractures
Concomitant injuries that require surgical management
Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management consists of knee immobilization in relative extension.

Techniques/Procedures
Arthrocentesis should be considered if a large hemarthrosis is present, and intra-
articular lidocaine injection to reduce pain may improve reduction and extension
position of knee immobilization.
The optimal amount of knee flexion for reduction is controversial; however, generally 0°
to 20° is recommended. Full extension may result in femoral condylar articulation on the
medial and lateral fracture margins assisting with maintenance of reduction, and
immobilization in full extension may reduce the risk of flexion contracture. Cast or brace
immobilization may be used for nonsurgical management.
Outcomes
Little long-term literature is available on the outcomes of nonsurgical management. Most
children are thought to do well, especially because most nonsurgically managed fractures are
of mild severity (ie, type I).
Surgical
Indications

Type II fractures that do not reduce with cast immobilization and type III fractures
Concomitant injuries requiring surgical management
Contraindications
Type I and reducible type II injuries without concomitant injuries that require surgical
management
Techniques/Procedures
The goal of surgical management is to restore stability of the ACL and remove any blocks to full
motion.
Open or arthroscopic reduction and internal fixation are options.
Type of fixation used (sutures versus suture anchors versus screws) often is determined by
fracture characteristics and surgeon preference (Resources 1 and 2).
Surgical Approach(es)
An open or arthroscopic approach can be utilized.

Surgical Approach(es)
Little robust data comparing surgical approaches are available. An open approach is
likely familiar to more surgeons and does not require special equipment but may result
in missed concomitant injuries because of inability to visualize the entirety of the joint.
This typically consists of a small parapatellar arthrotomy to directly manage the fracture.
An arthroscopic approach, although very useful in allowing for evaluation of the entire
joint for concomitant injuries, may be more technically demanding and requires special
instrumentation. Standard arthroscopic equipment is used for arthroscopic
management. Occasionally, accessory portals are helpful for suture management if
suture fixation is performed. Regardless of the approach (open versus arthroscopic), any
interposed tissue should be removed from the fracture site without damaging the
medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament. This may be facilitated by the placement
of a traction stitch in the intermeniscal ligament.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Fixation options include suture, suture anchors, screws, or other implants.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Various fixation methods are available, each of which is associated with advantages and
disadvantages; however, no one fixation method has been proven to be definitively
superior to others with high-level evidence.9 Regardless of the type of fixation, any
interposed tissue should be removed from the fracture site without damaging the
medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament. This may be facilitated by the placement
of a traction stitch in the intermeniscal ligament. In addition, provisional stabilization
with the use of a Kirschner wire may be helpful. Screw fixation involves direct
compression of the fragment, typically with the use of a cannulated implant. A
prominent screw head may impinge on the roof of the intercondylar notch, resulting in a
block to full extension. Screw fixation should avoid the physis or implant removal should
be planned. Comminuted fractures with small fracture fragments typically require suture
fixation. This typically involves securing the base of the ACL with the use of looped
sutures near the fracture fragment and passing the suture tails through small transtibial
tunnels to facilitate reduction (Figure 7). If substantial growth remains, these tunnels
should avoid the physis (Figure 8). The sutures are then tied over the tibia or
incorporated into a suture anchor or a cortical button. The current principles applicable
to any fixation technique are to provide stable fixation that restores ACL stability while
allowing for early motion.
Figure 7 Arthroscopic images of a knee show a tibial spine fracture (A) managed via
suture fixation (B). (Courtesy of Neeraj M. Patel, MD, MPH, MBS, Chicago, IL.)

Postoperative Management
Early motion is recommended to avoid arthrofibrosis.
Little evidence is available to guide weight-bearing status and return to sports activity after
surgical management of tibial spine fractures.

Postoperative Management
The primary goal of surgical management is to achieve bony union that restores ACL
stability and return to full function. Considerable debate exists with regard to optimal
rehabilitation after the fixation of tibial spine fractures. Some surgeons favor a shorter
rehabilitation protocol that is based mainly on fracture healing, whereas other surgeons
favor a longer rehabilitation protocol analogous to that for an ACL tear (ie, with a focus
on proprioception and neuromuscular control).
Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
The anterior horn of the medial meniscus or the intermeniscal ligament often is entrapped
and must be moved to allow for reduction (Resources 3 and 4).
The knee should be scrutinized closely for concomitant injuries.
Fixation should be stable enough to allow for early motion.
Complications
Arthrofibrosis is the most common complication after surgically and nonsurgically managed
tibial spine fractures. Early mobilization after surgical fixation reduces the risk.9-11
ACL laxity is common but generally not clinically important; however, studies have found an
increased risk of future ACL rupture after tibial spine fracture compared with the general
population.12

Persistent elevation of the anterior aspect of the fracture may result in impingement with the
intercondylar notch, resulting in pain or a block to full extension; however, in the absence of
symptoms or motion limitations, the importance of a small amount of residual anterior
elevation is unclear.
Nonunion generally is rare and may be avoided by ensuring stable fixation intraoperatively.
Growth arrest or angular deformity may result from rigid fixation that crosses the physis.
Outcomes
Little high-level, long-term literature is available on the outcomes of pediatric tibial spine
fractures. Most patients ultimately seem to do well (Figure 9); however, a high rate of
arthrofibrosis has been reported in the short term and an increased risk of ACL injury has
been reported in the long term in some patients.10,11,13

Pathophysiology/Pathoanatomy
Epidemiology
Tibial tubercle fractures account for less than 1% of physeal fractures. The mean age at injury
is 14 years (range, 13 to 16 years).
Anatomy and Biomechanics
Osteology
The proximal tibia has two ossification centers: the proximal tibial physis (primary center) and
the tubercle apophysis (secondary center).
As adolescents approach maturity, the physis first closes posteriorly and proximally, leaving
the tubercle apophysis to fuse last.
Vascular Anatomy
The recurrent anterior tibial artery may be injured with fracture of the tibial tubercle.

Vascular Anatomy
The recurrent anterior tibial artery is in the vicinity of the tibial tubercle. In patients with
a fracture, this artery may be injured and bleed into the surrounding compartment. This
may increase the risk of compartment syndrome.
Tendons
The patellar tendon attaches to the tibial tubercle.
Musculature
Because the tubercle is the attachment point of the patellar tendon, the entire extensor
mechanism, including quadriceps musculature, may exert force on the apophysis.

Fracture of the tibial tubercle typically is caused by concentric quadriceps contraction while
jumping or eccentric quadriceps contraction with forced knee flexion.

Etiology/Mechanism of Injury
Similar to the mechanism injury that may result in a patellar body fracture, patellar
tendon rupture, or patellar sleeve avulsion, tibial tubercle fractures often result from
eccentric quadriceps contraction. In adolescent patients, the tibial tubercle is more
vulnerable to injury than the patella, patellar tendon, and patellar chondral sleeve
because it is not yet fused.
Risk Factors
Adolescents in whom the proximal tibial physis has begun to close are at risk for this injury,
especially if participating in jumping or contact sports.
Associated Injuries
Associated injuries may be observed in approximately 4% of patients who have a fracture with
intra-articular extension14 (Resource 5).

Associated Injuries
Various associated injuries may be observed in patients with a tibial tubercle fracture.
The recurrent anterior tibial artery can be injured, resulting in excessive bleeding and
increased risk of compartment syndrome. Compartment syndrome also may be related
to bony bleeding under intact fascia. A portion of the extensor mechanism (ie, patellar
tendon, retinaculum, or periosteum) may be disrupted. A risk of meniscal or cartilage
injury exists if the fracture extends proximally into the knee joint (Resource 6).

Injury Classification
The Ogden classification is based on fracture morphology. Notably, type III fractures
involve the joint surface, and type IV fractures exit through the posterior tibial
metaphysis.
Mechanics of Fractures
The primary deforming force is the extensor mechanism, most often during eccentric loading.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Patients typically report an acute pop, often when jumping or during a contact injury.
Pain, swelling, difficulty bearing weight, and inability to actively extend the knee are common
complaints.
Physical Examination
Inspection of the injured extremity should focus on the degree of swelling and any skin tenting
because of fracture displacement. Specific attention should be paid to signs of compartment
syndrome.
The compartments of the leg, especially the anterior compartment, must be examined closely
because these fractures are associated with an increased risk of compartment syndrome if the
recurrent anterior tibial artery has been injured. In addition to assessment of a patient’s pain
and levels of anxiety and agitation, the physical examination should include assessment of the
firmness of the compartments, assessment for pain with passive ankle and toe stretch, and a
thorough neurovascular evaluation.
Patients report tenderness at the tibial tubercle. A palpable defect or deformity may be noted.
The integrity of the extensor mechanism should be evaluated if necessary but is not
recommended in patients with a displaced fracture. This can be accomplished by asking the

Patella alta may be observed because of the pull of the extensor mechanism on the patella
and the fracture fragment.
Neurovascular Examination
A baseline neurovascular examination is crucial in patients with a tibial tubercle fracture.
The quality of distal pulses and compartment firmness also must be noted. These must be
assessed serially, even after definitive management.

Neurovascular Examination
Although the five P’s (pain, pallor, paresthesia, pulselessness, and paralysis) may aid in
the detection of compartment syndrome in adults, the three A’s (increasing analgesic
requirement, anxiety, and agitation) may be more reliable signs of compartment
syndrome in children and adolescents.
Imaging Studies
Plain radiographs often are adequate in identifying the injury and guiding management.
Advanced imaging studies may be considered if the injury pattern is unclear or concern for
additional injuries exists.
Radiography
Plain radiographs typically are sufficient in diagnosing tibial tubercle fractures and guiding
management (Figure 11).

radiographs should be scrutinized for intra-articular extension. In addition, in patients
with a periosteal sleeve avulsion, the tubercle may appear nondisplaced; however,
radiographs should be evaluated for patella alta.

Management
Nonsurgical Management
Indications
Nonsurgical management may be performed in patients with minimally displaced fractures
and no extensor lag.

Indications
Nonsurgical management is indicated for minimally displaced fractures or those with no
extensor lag. The specific displacement threshold for surgical versus nonsurgical
management is unclear based on the existing literature. For intra-articular fractures, 2
mm often is used as a cutoff value. If questions exist with regard to displacement or
angulation, radiographs of the contralateral knee can be obtained to compare patellar
height and the posterior tibial slope. Fractures with extension through the posterior
metaphysis (ie, inverted, U-shaped fracture pattern) are at increased risk of additional
displacement with nonsurgical management.16

Techniques/Procedures
Nonsurgical management consists of knee immobilization.

Techniques/Procedures
Immobilization of the knee may involve a cast (long leg cast or cylinder cast) or a brace,
depending on physician preference and patient adherence. Little evidence is available to
guide optimal weight-bearing status, the duration of immobilization, and the
rehabilitation protocol.
Outcomes
Minimal data are available on the long-term results of nonsurgically managed tibial tubercle
fractures.

Indications
Surgical treatment is recommended for children who have a displaced fracture and/or an
extensor lag.

as a cutoff value. If questions exist with regard to displacement or angulation,
radiographs of the contralateral knee can be obtained to compare patellar height and

Techniques/Procedures
Open reduction with screw fixation for fracture types I through IV.
For type III fractures, the joint should be visualized to accurately reduce the articular surface
and to assess for meniscal injury.
Suture reattachment of the periosteal sleeve, which may be supplemented with the use of
small screws, is the preferred technique for type V fractures.
Preoperative Planning
Radiographs should be scrutinized for intra-articular extension of the fracture.
If joint surface involvement is noted, then a small arthrotomy may be required to adequately
visualize the joint surface and meniscus. Arthroscopy also may be considered for intra-
articular assessment; however, this must be performed with caution to prevent excessive
fluid extravasation into a limb that may already be at increased risk for compartment
syndrome.
The trajectory of the fracture should be assessed to plan optimal screw positioning.

Preoperative Planning
In addition to planning screw trajectory, preoperative imaging studies should be
evaluated to assess fracture fragment number, size, and location. Some fractures may
consist of multiple bony fragments. Any fragments that are particularly small or thin
should be considered in planning implant type and position.
Patient Positioning
The patient is placed in the supine position on a radiolucent table with a small bump under the
ipsilateral hip. A radiolucent triangle also may be helpful.

Surgical Approaches
A direct approach is used. Lavage and curettage of fracture hematoma and sharp
excision of periosteal margins of the fracture should be employed while preserving
fracture anatomy. Given the mostly unfused nature of the tubercle in adolescents, the
undersurface of the fracture fragment may be cartilaginous. The patellar tendon should
be inspected for avulsion from the fragment and repaired if indicated. Therapeutic or
prophylactic fasciotomies should be performed if concern for compartment syndrome
exists.
Surgical Fracture Fixation
At least two screws typically are required for stable fixation. Rarely, crossed Steinmann pins
are indicated to supplement screw fixation.
Suture constructs with anchors can be used for thin or comminuted fractures in which screw
fixation may result in fragment comminution
Suture constructs via drill holes or suture anchors can be used for patellar sleeve avulsions.

Surgical Fracture Fixation
Little high-quality data are available on cannulated versus solid screws, optimal screw
size, indications for the use of washers, and bicortical versus unicortical screws. Larger
screws may provide more rigid fixation but, theoretically, may result in more implant
prominence and irritation. This can be minimized by countersinking the screw heads and
ensuring adequate soft-tissue coverage. Headless screws may be considered as an
alternative; however, little data are available on this technique. Washers may be useful in
fixing thin fracture fragments. At least one retrospective study suggests bicortical screws
are not always necessary for all tubercle fractures17 Unicortical screws may decrease the
risk of iatrogenic popliteal artery injury during screw placement (Figure 12). If fracture
fragments are too diminutive or fragile for direct screw fixation, the patellar tendon can
be sutured with the fragments incorporated. The tails of these sutures can then be fixed
into the proximal tibia with the use of suture anchors or by passing through an

Postoperative Management
Wide variation exists in postoperative protocols after fixation of tibial tubercle fractures. Most
commonly, a several-week period of postoperative immobilization is recommended.
Soft-tissue repair of sleeve avulsions may require longer immobilization.

Debate exists regarding optimal weight bearing, the duration of immobilization, the
need for formal physical therapy, and the time frame for return to sports

Pitfalls and Preventative Measures
Regardless of the screw size and configuration used, implant and fracture stability should be
assessed via fluoroscopy and direct visualization before leaving the operating room.
Close attention must be paid to the possibility of compartment syndrome, especially
preoperatively. Fasciotomies should be performed if compartment syndrome is suspected or
confirmed.
Iatrogenic injury to the popliteal artery may be avoided by placing unicortical screws if
possible.
For thin or comminuted fracture fragments in which robust screw fixation is not possible, the
construct can be supplemented with the use of Krackow-type sutures in the extensor
mechanism that are then fixed with the use of suture anchors or through a bone tunnel
distally.
Complications
Compartment syndrome is the most concerning complication; however, it is uncommon if
appropriate physical examination, monitoring, and surgical management are performed.14,18
Genu recurvatum may result from premature closure of the tubercle apophysis and/or bar
formation of the anterior physis and may result in a decrease in the posterior tibial slope.
Because of the transitional age in which this fracture normally occurs, this may be a clinically
relevant concern only in a minority of younger patients.
Vascular injury may be related to the fracture itself or iatrogenic injury that occurs
intraoperatively.
Implant prominence is the most common complication and may necessitate screw removal.14
Stiffness or arthrofibrosis may occur with prolonged immobilization.
Rehabilitation
Wide variation exists in postoperative protocols after fixation of tibial tubercle fractures. Most
protocols involve an initial period of immobilization postoperatively. Typically, 4 weeks or less

Little high-quality, long-term data are available on children and adolescents treated for a tibial
tubercle fracture. A meta-analysis of mostly level IV studies found that most children were able
to regain full motion and return to preinjury level of activity.14
